retrieved.title: Moot court notes
retrieved.text:
Moot court notes: "This house would adopt a nationwide four-day work week" V. Hale, for the Meridian Bar Society exhibition debate. Private notes.

¶ 1. Expect the opposition to say the evidence base is narrow. Concede scope early, then shift the burden: the status quo is also a policy and has to justify itself.

¶ 2. Historical anchor: the Meridian Working Hours Act 1931 made the two-day weekend the default. It gave agriculture and shipping a ten-year transition and exempted continuous services.

¶ 3. Continuous-coverage sectors already run on shift rules under Part IV of the Working Time Code: rest periods, a cap on consecutive shifts, and averaging over a reference period. A shorter standard week sits inside that structure.

¶ 4. Phase-in precedent: sector-by-sector timetables, collective agreements first, the public sector as model employer. Courts have upheld staged duties where the end point is clear.

messages.content: Schools are where kids spend most of their waking hours, and phones turn that time into a slot machine. I'd ban them during school hours because the evidence on attention is solid: a buzzing phone in a pocket pulls focus even when it's not in use, and that hits the kids who are already struggling hardest. Second, the social pressure to be reachable and performing online never takes a break in a phone-permitted school. Third, this is enforceable and teachable — clear hours, clear rule. That's not punishment. It's giving kids a room where they can actually think.

Three points, and I shall keep them tight. First, define your terms: a ban is not guidance, not a norm, not a bell rung at the classroom door; it is state coercion applied to every pupil, and coercion demands a burden of proof its proponents have not carried. Second, a school is not a sovereign: it may regulate conduct within its gates, but a blanket prohibition substitutes a rule for the harder work of teaching judgment, and judgment is the thing phones actually require. Third, and decisively, the motion forbids the tool rather than the distraction. If a device disrupts a lesson, the school may already confiscate it; if it does not, the ban punishes the innocent to inconvenience the guilty. Define your terms, Kai, and the ban collapses under its own breadth.

Banning phones outright is the policy version of a single-number answer, and I don't trust it. The evidence on learning is mixed and mostly correlational: effects cluster around zero to modest, and they look largest for already-disengaged students. My worry is second-order: take phones out of classrooms and supervision migrates into corridors, canteens, and homes, and it lands hardest on kids whose phones are their main lifeline. So I'd regulate use by age and context, not confiscate a device.

What's still open is the thing neither of my colleagues has answered: what a ban actually costs, and who pays. Amara gets a cleaner classroom; Victor gets a narrower rule. Both are real, and both are modest. My position is the stronger one because it survives the comparison — targeted restriction captures most of the attention gain without confiscating the lifeline, and it doesn't pretend a rule substitutes for teaching judgment. If you want one number, you're being sold something. The honest range still favours regulation.

Mei's right that I owe an answer on cost, so here it is: I don't get a cleaner classroom without paying for it, and I won't pretend otherwise. Some kids lose a lifeline during school hours. That's a real cost, and it's why I'd pair the ban with working school phones, staffed offices, and accommodation for kids with genuine medical or caregiving needs. But targeted regulation has a cost too, and it's the one Mei hasn't priced: who enforces "age and context" at the door, in every corridor, every day? That discretion lands hardest on the same kids. The ban's strength is that it's honest about what it is — bounded hours, clear rule, exceptions built in, no pretending the rule replaces teaching judgment. Let's figure out what's actually going on.

Two things remain open, and neither rescues the ban. First, the enforcement question Amara concedes she owes us: she says "bounded hours, clear rule, exceptions built in" — but exceptions are precisely where the discretion she condemns in Mei's proposal lives, now laundered through a nurse's note and an office stamp. Second, and decisive, nobody has met the definitional burden I set in opening: a ban is prohibition, and no one has shown the school's ordinary authority to confiscate a distracting device is insufficient. Strip the rhetoric and you have a narrower, cheaper rule that achieves the same classroom.
